By Cable to The Star and Chicago Daily News.


COPENHAGEN, September "A
curious fight has started between the
Copenhagen bakers and the assotia-
ton called the Consumers Guard. The
bakers have raised their prices on
several kinds of bread and the asso-
citation has protested saying there has
been no reason for increasing prices.


Consumers Guard members num-
bering several thousand sent a petit
ton to the government. asking aid,
but the government, although agree
ing that prices of bread were too
high. refused assistance. Now the
guard has declared a strike, asking
not only their own members, but the
whole population of Copenhagen not
to buy bread at the increased rates
and start home baking. Several thou
sand people participated in the strike,
but the bakers have declined to lower
their charges. saying bread cannot
be sold cheaper. The result of the
strike is being awaited with much
anxiety.

MENICO CITY, August 4.-Federal
forces are searching for the slayers
of Mrs. Rosalie Evans. who was shot
dead from ambush near Texmelucan,
Puebla, Saturday night.


The widow of a British subject.
a former president of the Bank of
London in Mexico, Mrs. Evans was
one of the central figures in the re-
cent international affair between
Great Britain and Mexico, eliminating
in the withdrawal of the British
charge des archives, Herbert c. Cum
Minis. MIR. Cummins was accused by
the Mexicans of undue harshness in
his communications concerning AIRS.
Evans dispute with the Mexican gov
ernment over attempts to divide her
estate under the agrarian program.


Accompanied by John Strauss, the
German manager of her estate, Mrs.
Evans was driving homeward, when
shots came from the left and she
fell from the wagon. Her hair be-
came entangled in the wheels and
the body was dragged some distance,





made a desperate effort to defend his
employer, but was wounded in the
arm and forced to abandon the fight
He managed, however, to release her
body from the wheels and summon
help before colIapsing.


U. s. Envoy in Case.


American Charge d'Affaires Schoen-
field last night conferred with For
eign Minister Saenz. He said later
that they discussed the details of
the attack. but he was otherwise un-
communicative. Representatives of
the British consulate general have
gone to Texmelucan to bring the body
to Mexico City.


Mrs. Evans six-year fight to hold
her hacienda, consisting of 1850
hectares (about 436 acres) and called
San Pedro Coxtocan, has been fol-
lowed with intense interest in diplo-
matte circles and in both the British
and American colonies. Mrs Evans
was formerly of Brownsville, Tex.


The question figured in the pre-
recognition conferences last Summer,
when the American delegates unoffi-
cial efforts succeeded in bringing
about meeting between Mrs. Evans
and President Obregon. Several
months ago. when word reached the
capital that the hacienda was sur
rounded by armed agrarians, volun-
teers from the British colony visited
Puebla to help protect the owner.


She personally waged a fearless
fight, several times driving invaders
off her land at pistol point. She in
sisted on living in the ruined ranch
house, which had been burned, and,
besides her employees, was protected
by George Camp, a Texan, who aban-
doned his contracting business here
several months ago to go to the ha-
cienda- His present whereabouts is
unknown.


Official admission that the Evans
case had been taken over by the
American embassy came several
weeks after Charge Cummins' de-
parture, when Ambassador Warren
said Mrs. Evans had laid the entire
question before him. The Mexican
governments stand has always been
that Mrs. Evans was making obsti-
nate and unjustifiable resistance to
it's plans for the division of her es-
tate under the governmental agra
rian program, with proper remunera-
tion to her.

Another Harvard astronomical sta

continuous Photographic patrol of

excellent work in its astronomical

made of celestial objects south of the
equator. But the weather is often

They are hopping along, those in
trepid American globe flyers. Long
delayed in the icy regions Of Iceland
and Greenland, they are now coming
south rapidly. Yesterday they took
off from Ice Tickle, Labrador, despite
rain and fog, and landed in Hawkes.
Bay, Newfoundland. Today they move
on to Pictou, Nova Scotia, and tomor-
row they hop to Boston, where they
will drop their pontoons and don their
earth-landing wheels. This means that
they may reach Washington Saturday
or perhaps Sunday.


They are now in hurry, these
globe flyers, fastening home after the
worst Of their long journey. Little
things like wind squalls and rain and
fog are not holding them back now.
They have flown over great stretches
of the sea, over mountains and over
deserts. They are back in civilization.
They are making real globe-circling
time, and if pressed could make bet.
ter time. But it is well to proceed with
some caution. A mishap at this stage
OF the journey would be especially
lamentable. They have gone nearly
around the world with no fatalities,
though two of the planes have
dropped out Of the race. They hope
to make goal with no further diminu.

worldwide struggle, poor Spanish Flor
ida.


Here a large Indian nation, once
civilized, but now reduced to savage
ry, had taken refuge from the Ameri-
cans: and these people, the Creeks
and Seminoles, fighting for freedom
themselves, gave shelter to runaway
slaves from the United States. few

and some Scottish gentlemen lived with

haps to them, Great Britain armed

settlements to the north, and at Fort

Northward in Tennessee the militia
were commanded by Andrew jackson,
born n frontiersman, but by trade
lawyer very valiant man of high
renown, truculent as n bantam.


Without orders he led two thousand
five hundred frontiersmen to avenge
Fort Minns by chasing the Spanish
governor Tin time of peace) out of
Pensacola, and British garrison from
Fort Barrancas, and then (after peace
was signed) expelled the British from
New Orleans, while his detachment
in Florida blew up a fort with two
hundred seventy-five refugees. Such
was the auspiclous prelude to Jack
sons war with the Creeks, who were
crushed forever at the battle of Horse
shoe Bend.

wonderful The development of new

welcomed all over the circuit this
season.

Special Dispatch to The Star.


VICTORIA, British Columbia. Octo-
ber 9.-As the American liner Presi-
dent Grant was leaving Hongkong
harbor on the voyage which brought
her here recently Chinese small boat,
OF sampan, suddenly cut across her
bows. The big passenger ship crash
ed sQuarely into the tiny craft. 1t
sank in a few seconds and the men,
bers Of the Chinese crew were taken
aboard the American ship. To the
amazement of the ships officers, they
appeared delighted with their expert
ence.


Inquiry through an interpreter
ELECTED the announcement that the
President Grant had done the Chinese
a service of incalculable value-it had
destroyed a devil which had been fol-
lowing the -sampan insistently for
months. The important thing was
that the devil had been killed for
good. When the Chinese got a new
boat they would be able to travel
without a monster trailing them.


The sampan, the crew explained,
had been guided across the bows of
the liner purposely. When a Chinese
boat thus crosses a big ship, they
said, the devil naturally is cut away
by the towering bow of the liner.

markets. Decreases

other groups except foods showed
decrease.

milk, wool and tobacco, while in
metals, iron and steel products, cop
per, lead, tin and zinc averaged less
than in April. Many other important
raw commodities showed price de-
creases.

fresh meats, -four and certain fruits
offset the decreases reported for
other articles, leaving the general

convicted associate broke the silence
for them.'

and Sullivan were ignored, pending

authorities and population of Lenin-

the way they have met and fought

every class rose to the occasion. all
working with the utmost of good
Will There WAS no violence, no

In saying this. the correspondent

outside the Winter Palace there

whole districts swept away. Tues

mark on the same plaque, but the
number of drowned is trivial com
pared with 1924. The present stone
houses stood much better than the
houses of 1924. but for material loss
1924 makes 1924 sink into insignifi-

ships and boats on the river and

Wind CapriciouS.

aster which has overtaken Lenin

So it ei1ded-Chickie's first step
on the road back. 1t came as she
was beginning to find the sun
golden again; q flower along the
way.


And this exposure was more
terrible than the first because it
was prophetic. It foretold with
ruthless candor, her future.


She need have no doubt now
as to the worlds attitude.
She had broken the law. She
had loved and brought her child
here without. permission.


Did she think this slight mat
ter? Did she think she could
erect q little stone above the
dead baby's grave; make up
name for It; push her own hurts
far down under valiant smile
and then come back? Put out
her hands to Life and say: "Oh.
Life, it's done and past: let me
try again-please"? Did she
think she could reach out her
hands like that as though ner
hands were clean?


she did. For Chickie's heart was
q soft and glowing thing. It had
never seen the evil Of her sin as
the world saw It; never felt itself
all shame and degradation be-
cause of having loved. Oh, it
had fine, eager pulses made for
Joy. They could throb yet.


So her heart had hoped, even
when her mind. so deeply hurt
in its young pride, was beaten.
1t had hoped on as vivid hearts
will, but now 1t too was schooled;
it, too, had learned.


Thine world did not want it;
the world would not have it.
Chickie lay on her bed, her face
hidden in the pillows. 1t seemed
that thousand tons were
upon her, pressing and pressing.
She could never rise; shake them
free.


Again and again she went
though the scenes: Edith Pot
ter confronting her with that
cold, enraged look, then walking
up and stripping the basket from
Chickie's arm. AS though
thing whose presence had defiled
their home; whose coming was
an outrage to friendship.


The memory burned. It was
a great scarlet wound that
spread until there was neither
fight nor pride left in Chickie's
thoughts. She saw herself as all
of them were seeing her.


Oh-she could hear Myra King
with the high color blazing in
her cheeks, her small eyes
squirting: hear Myra say: Can
you imagine 1t! Passing herself
off for one Of us! She was per.
fectly notorious-every one got
to know 1t. A child? Why-of
course. Died-that never was
cleared up-the whole thing q
mystery. All the papers had 1t.
Just fancy coming down here
and palming herself off the
way she did! Almost got away
away with it!


And Chiclie could see In her
tortured imagination the indignant
yet gloating eyes. hear the eager
questions.


when? Just imagine that!
Well-if 1t were years past, one
might understand! Did you ever
know Of anything so brazen?
Why. one would think butter
wouldn't melt in her mouth! 1t
wouldn't be so bad If she'd been
humble about 1t. but breeding
around pushing herself into
thingsw


There was no end to It. Her
thoughts found new terms for
the condemnation; brought new
images Of stained and brazen
thing before her until she grew
frightened and cowed at the
thought Of herself, until it SEEM
ed that going there. being what
she was, made her shame mon.
strous: made her utterly lost.


Never-she could never raise
her head again; never beat off
thC WCA6hl Va tAAlc JOu6 IlCuS. II
was a yoke. She grew limp
under its weight.


She dreamed Of Luis Lamarck,
awakened with a rude. ugly ter
ror: feeling the mans sleek
eyes going over her. She had
dreamed that as he placed his
hand on hers, Edith standing at
the car, called. Don't Luis!
Don't touch herr Luis had
smiled; his hand had felt along
Chickie's arm.


The next morning she had
scarcely strength to dress. She
sat at her window until noon:
leaving the bed unmade; her hair
uncombed. She was afraid to
think.

BY Cable to The Star and Chicago Daily News.


VIENNA. October 22.-By sending
a large number of troops along the
Russian frontier, Poland and Rumania
have mastered the band situation,
which had become serious.


Exceedingly well organized and
equally well armed rowing bands were
accustomed to invade Poland and
Rumania from the Russian side of
their borders. Owing to the sparse
population in the unfortile, sandy
region which is covered with pine
forests, they were able to operate
a long time without interference,
ro5bing the farms and villages.


Although the bands come from
Russia 1t is not thought that the
Soviets are responsible, but rather
that their activities were the result
of internal conditions there.


There still remain many unsettled
questions between the border states
and Russia, but Tchitcherin has signf-
fed his readiness to negotiate.

The Coast Guards war on rum
runners is in full swing. and the op-
erations of many of its boats this
week have met with success.


Although Coast Guard headquarters
has insisted upon strict observance of
it's order to maintain secrecy about
its work of chasing rum runners and
other smugglers, its official organ, the
Weekly Bulletin, issued yesterday.
carries a list Of citations of crews
who have captured prisoners and
seized liquor and other contraband.
Indications were given also that in
chasing down rum runners. Coast
guardsmen more than once had to
use their guns in defense against the
gunfire Of the runners.


Gunrd Ships Rammed.


One new method employed by the
rum runners also was disclosed.
When several have been near capture
and efforts at escape seemed fruit
less, proWs OF the speedy liquor boats
have been turned straight into the
lighter Coast Guard craft, and they
were ramned. On two occasions at
least Coast Guard boats had grea.
holes torn in their hulls, but the rum
runners were captured.


The Weekly Bulletin lists among
others the capture of the American
motor boat Viking, with 35 cases of
ale, and the taking of one prisoner
Personnel from the Seabright station
took the motor boat Lynx II, with
500 cases of liquor and five prison
ers, after a running fight, in which
the master of the rum runner was
killed. The master of the motor boat
Adventure was wounded during a
chase which made that craft a prize
for the Coast Guard of the Hereford
Inlet station.

found by the Fairport station at
Richmond. Ohio, far away from snug

cargo of liquor. Coast Guard Off

craft has been seized along the Ohio
and Mississippi Rivers in attempts to
carry the trade further inland.
Stories around Coast Guard head
quarters are to the effect that snug
glers are increasing their efforts

Ages were revived last night at the
picturesque Twelfth Night party
given by Mr.. and Mrs. John Hays
Hammond for their debutante
daughter, Miss Natalie Hammond.
knights and ladies came together
then to hobnob with Robin Hood
and his merry men; crusaders rub.
bed elbows with 'friars in girdled
habits and heroes and heroines Of
history and romance.


The spacious home Of Mr.. and
Mrs. Hammond, with it's stone faced
walls and its great fire place In
which Yule logs were burning, made
an effective setting for the colorful
assemblage. And. under the magic
hand Of James Reynolds-who has
devised some Of the loveliest scenes
for 1.-THE Folliee," and who is widely
known in Washington for his imag-
NATIVE work with the RAMS Head
Players-the great house had been
transformed into a veritable castle
of the Middle Ages. Great banners
of scarlet and gold contributed a
glowing note of color, walls were
Rarlanded with laurel leaves and





replaced the usual lights.


The revels began with a dinner
for seventy guests, all young people
and all in medieval costume. After
ward there was q delightful musical
given by Frank and Elizabeth Sher-
idan and Esther Case. They were
in old world costume and their
program was made up OF songs or
Medieval days. Interesting fear
lures thereof were the arrangements
of Elizabethan songs by Richard
Hammond, son Of Mr.. and Mrs.
Hammond, which were charmingly
sung by Mrs. Sheridan and Miss
Case.


For the recital a number of addi-
tional guests were asked, and they
of course, were not in fancy cos
tune, so that modern and medieval
were mingled in picturesque effect


The guests for dinner were
seated about a table laid in the
form of a hollow square, covered
with q scarlet cloth and decked out
with boar's heads, sucking pigs
and great masses of rosy fruits
Ancient tones had been searched
for medieval recipes. and such
viands were served as spiced eggs
venison pasties, sorrel and rose
mary apples. A procession OF stall
wart henchmen in medieval dress
bearing aloft the boar's head and
all the famous old-time dishes
made it's way about the table as the
guests were being seated.


Between the courses many diver
sions typical Of the old-time cele'
bration of Twelfth Night-the time
when the Three Kings came bea".
Ting gifts to the Christ Child in the
Manger-were worked in. There
was a soothsayer-W. c. Norman,
assisted by Miss Martha Davis
who read a prophecy, for each OF
| the guests, and heralds in scarlet,
white and goId-Mr. Loveless and
Mr.. Duval-introduced the various
features Of the entertainment. This
part of the program was under the
direction of John p. j. Mulvane,
president of the Caravan Club.
Mrs. Hammond wore an up-to.
date evening gown OF black ana
gold brocade, but there was a hint
of the medieval in the flowing
sleeves Of scarlet chiffon, which
was borne out by the veil OF rare
black lace helR in place by a mag
nificent jeweled comb.


Miss Natalie Hammond wore a
lovely costume Of heavy rose col
ored silk, banded with gold and
girdled with jewels. A court train
of gorgeous brocade in which rich
rose. blues and green were mingled
with q CLINT Of gold, was hung
from the shoulders. Pearls were
twined in her hair which hung
in two long braids over her shout
ders and her rosy veil fell from a
1eweled circlet. Miss Elizabeth
Hammond also made a charming
picture in a flowing flame colored
robe, banded with fur, with a
medieval headdress Of cloth Of gold
sewn with jewels.


Other charming figures in the

nolds in black hose and golden

drawn match against each other.

crew and the lacrosse team. The

leys and was defeated by Yale and

outs.

land, Johns Hopkins and Syracuse.

punitive expedition has been carried
out by the Italian forces in the Oasis
of Gialo against the rebel organiza-
ton formed by the Senussi Arabs.

villages of Fehrra and Lebba on the
oasis for half an hour, while the
Arabs below subjected them to a sus-
tanned rifle fire. One of the planes
was struck five times without suffer-
ing serious damage.

great difficulty because of the dis
tance from this center and because of
bad visibility. The two airplanes.
however, crossed the desert, bonn
barded the rebels and returned to
Bengazi after having flown distance
of approximately 373 miles and hav-
ing remained in the air eight hours.


The authorities believe that the
expedition, besides material results of
the bomba rdment of the aviators, will
undoubtedly have a great moral ef-
feet on the population of Cirenaica.
Since d'Annunzio's flight over Vienna
this is regarded as the most auda-
cious attempt made by Italian army
aviators.

ST. JOHNS, Newfoundland, June
2O.--Out Of the fog-shrouded North
Atlantic came a story today OF how
presence Of mind and devotion to
duty saved probably 1000 lives
when the Canadian Pacific liner
Metagama was nearly cut In two in
collision with the Italian steamship
Clara Campus in thick curtain Of
mist seven miles off Cape Race.


Both vessels, the MetagaHna carry
Ing 1000 passengers, were creeping
through the fog Wednesday, when
the Italian ship struck the other
steamer aTnidship, tearing a huge
hole in her hull.


So serious was the. accident that
the officers Of the Canadian liner
feared she could not make shore,
and began Immediately to send out
20. o. S." calls.


Other vessels turned from their
course, but owing to the thick
weather had difficulty in reaching
the scene Of the accident.


Water Fills Hold.


The Metagama began q thrilling
race for safety.


While the hold filled with water,
the vessel was turned toward shore,
but could only creep, owing to the
thick fog and the severe list to
starboard. The pumps were kept
working at the highest pressure.
while officers went among the pas
sengers assuring them that they
were safe.


throughout the entire night
- Avak -
almost impenetrable mist, the vessel
crawled towards land. It appeared
to be a losing fight. for the water
kept gaining continuously over the
pumps.


AZ last, after a twenty.four hour
battle, the Metagama made port
and was beached. Officers said she
was saved ''by q few yards" as the
water in the huh had nearly
reached the limit, destroying the
ships "buoyance."


Sailors Lost In Boat.


Despite the danger to themselves
and their charges, officers did not
neglect the italian ship. They sent
three sailors from the Metagama to
find out how badly the Clara Cam.
pus had been damaged. They got
lost in the fog and failed to- reach
the Italian vessel. Nor could they
find their way back to the Meta.
CANA, and their fate is unknown.


The Clara Campus reached port
shortly after the Metagama. with
her bows badly crumped.


While the Canadian ship was
creeping toward port, the Red Cross
liner, Rosalind, attracted by the
wireless calls. came up and con.
voyed her part Of the way.

The crescent of the little beach was
like a silver bow. Far out over the
glistening waters stretched the gleam-
ing pathway of the moon. The tide
was on the turn and each succeeding
wave tossed glittering jewels nearer
to our feet. The moon had lightly
touched the sands and transformed
them to grains of the purest silver;
she had changed a prosaic rowboat to
a ship of dreams. Above us the depth
of the inky sky was thickly inlaid
with golden stars. Other stars, nearer
the horizon, were caught and held by
the sea as, huddled close together,
they vainfy strove to vie with their
loftier brethren. The little rlpples
seemed to be sharing some delightful
secret. We could hear them whisper
ing together about 1t, and when they
met and played among the rocks they
chuckled gleefully. Who cares for
the silver and gold of merchandise,
with Its cllnk and jangle? Richer far,
Is he that holds the memory of one
precious hour when words were not
spoken, but felt, when silence brooded,
fraught with meaning, and the soft,
sweet chuckles of the waves were the
only voices. An hour all inwrought
with natures silver and gold.

Capt. Donald B. Macmillan, noted
Arctic explorer, brings back from his
latest journey into the Polar regions
word that the ice cap about the North
Pole is growing steadily larger, and
that glaciers are moving steadily
southwark. This information, while
intensely interesting to the layman,
is Of tremendous Importance to the
scientist.


That the earth has undergone four
great ice ages and one period of pro-
longed chill there seems to be no
doubt, If we rely upon an abundance
of geological data The last one,
which some biologists says ended
about $4,000 years ago, left its mark
about st. Louis and all the northern
part of North America. But between
each of the so-called ice ages that
antedated the last one, the ice caps
and glaciers entirely disappeared.
leaving the earth tropic and temper
ate over its entire surface. This
probably accounts for the coal
forests, the tropical fora, that have
become the bituminous deposits Mac
MILAN found 500 miles from the
North Pole.


His observations seem to substan-
tiate the opinion of some scientists
that the period between ice ages is
shortening. that the Polar ice caps
and the glaciers of the world are
the shrunken remains of the last
great north Polar ice cap and the
movement of it's glaciers is the begin
ming of another era which eventually
will be thousands of feet under huge
glaciers.


But the scientist has a word of en-
couragement-it would be many gen.
erations before the new era arrives

BENWOOD, w. Va, April 2o-
-lhe smoking mouth of Vulture
Hollow mine today began to give up
Its shattered victims. Rescue squads,
after penetrating more than half
way back, sent out word that prob
ably not soul had lived to tell of
the explosion yesterday.


One hundred and eleven men had
been checked into the pit only few
minutes before the blast thundered
through its darkened tunnels. All
that was left of forty-fve of them
had been found at dawn today, burn
ed and broken bodies, sprawline
where they had been trapped with
out d minutes notice.


Rescue squads gathered here from
est Virginia, Maryland Pennsylya-
mia and Ohio were straining anew to
dlsentomb the seventy-one others, but
the farther the sappers penetrated
the more hopeless became the pros
pect that any could have lived All
but two of the victims found thus far
died in their tracks, many with their
picks in their hands.


Deadly Gas Inside.


The blast that swept through the
mine, which is operated by the Wheel
ing Steel Corporation, was accompanied
by momentary but terrific fire, and
the bodies of the men were scared hor-
ribly, besides being battered by the I'M
pact of the explosion. What mine
experts declare finally seal the doom
of any possible survivors are choking
vapors of deadly gases.


Only two of the men found thus
far showed sign of life. They were
discovered only 800 feet from the air
shaft through which the rescuers are
digging their way. Both were breath
ing family, but before DIR. A. B.
Rhinehart could get them out to the
fresh air they died and their bodies
were left where they were found.


Working Near Shaft.


Those two miners had been work.
ing close to the air shaft and the
explosion had been sufficiently spent
when it reached them to spare them
instantaneous death. They had drag
ged their battered bodies several hun
dred feet after being felled, but before
they could reach the safety of the





killed them.


Several hundred feet back the first
rescue squads to penetrate the wall
of debris the explosion piled up came
upon the bodies of a section boss and
his son. The boy had been holding
a light for his father while the
parent hacked at a vein of coal with
his pick and each was found stark
dead just as he had worked.


Bodies Crowded Together.


AS the sappers penetrated few
yards at a time the bodies were
found at closer intervals and two
crews of five men each were lying
together in death; even in the side
passages. where mine officials had
hoped some of the men may have
had time to barricade themselves,
only twisted victims and staggering
gas fumes awaited the anxious calls
of the rescuerS.


Vulture Hollow, where the air shaft
sinks three hundred feet into the
bowels of the earth, is at the end of
a road that is so precipitous and so
muddy that it is impossible to all but
even the hardest mixers. There the
rescue squads have pitched their
tents and are working in shifts.


Tell Horrible Stories.


Every few minutes a rescuer was
dragged out more dead than alive and
between gasps they told stories that
staggered the imagination and left
their listeners pale. One carried in his
hand a bit of twisted tin that was
once a miners lunch pail. Scarcely
able to talk, he gesticulated toward
the crushed pail and said:


Look in il. look in it. My God, it
must have been awful"


Inside were several sandwiches and
Two hard-boiled eggs. The bread of
toasted and the eggs were smashed TO
bits by the explosion. Others carried
out pieces of lunch pals that had been
blown to bits. Even pick handles
were snapped off short and the roof
of the mine was blown down into The
Dassageways in many places


Gas Overcomes Birds.


Half a dozen canary birds carried
into unexplored tunnels by advance
squads were brought to the surface
living unconscious in their cages. All,
however, had been hurried out into
the air before life had ceased to exist
and they were soon revived, and each
brought mute message OF the hope
iessness of the situation.


"There isn't a chance that any of
Hhese men are alive" was the unani-
nous verdict of the rescuers as they
we're helped to the surface to rest
for few minutes beside a warm
:.amp fire and drink hot, stimulating
S,offee before donning gas masks again
and return to the dogged task of
5oring a new tunnel through the
debris.

Testimony which would tend to
eSonerate Prohibition Agent Otis
E. Fisher of the charge of shoot
ing Senator Frank L. Greene, dur
ing a recent pistol battle on Penn
sylvania avenue, was given before
a special House subcommittee in
vestigating law and order in the
District.


Mrs. Greene, wife of the SEN
ator, told her version of the shoot
ing. She was confused as to the
details, but gave testimony which
indicated that the shot which
struck the Senator was fired by
bootleggers, who were attempting
to make their escape and not by
Fisher.


Her Testimony Brief.


Mrs. Greene was on the stand for
but few minutes. She was not
closely questioned by members of
the committee. She testified that
she was walking with the Senator
along Pennsylvania avenue toward
the Hotel Driscoll when the affair
occurred. AS they neared the mouth
of an alley, Jackson Hall alley, she
heard q report which she at first
thought was an automobile back
fire, but which she later became
convinced was a pistol shot or a
group of pistol shots. She did not
hear the shot fired at the time Sem
ator Greene was struck, nor did
she see the man who fired the shot.


The chief witness for the COM
mittee was Detective Michael J.
Dowd, Of the Sixth precinct. Dowd
declared that the bootleg car, from
which the first shots were fired,
was coming out of the alley and
that Fisher stood between the car
and Pennsylvania avenue near the
mouth Of the alley with his back
turned to the Avenue.


Fired Away From Greene.


His testimony led members of the
committee to believe that the shot
which struck Senator Greene was
fired by the bootleggers at Fisher
and that it struck the Senator
after rebounding from a wall.


At the time the Senator was shot,
Dowd's testimony indicated Fishers
back was turned to the Senator
and any shots he might have fired
at that time were fired away from,
rather than towards, the victim.

By the Associated Press.


LONDON, June 25.-Baron Arnold
undersecretary for colonies, informed
the House of Lords yesterday that
the British government had instruct
ed it's amba assador at Washington 10
inform the United States government
that Great Britain had reached the
conclusion it is desirable that the
conduct of matters at Washington eX-
cluSively relating to the Irish Free
State should be entrusted to minis
ter plenipotentiary accredited to the
United States. He added the govern
ment trusted this proposal would be
acceptable to the United States.


Explains Minister'S Status.


Lord Arnold went into a full ex-
PLANTATION of the status of the minis
ter. should the United States con-
sent The governments action in
the matter was based upon a prece-
dent set in 1920. when it was agreed
that Canada might be separately rep
resented at Washington.


The minister would be appointed
by the Free State government and
receive his credentials in the usual
manner from the king. Both docu-
ments would make it clear that the
appointment was solely for dealing
with Free State concerns.


Plans Made to Avoid Conflict.


Lord Arnold further explained that
careful provisions had been made
governing the relations between the
British and Free State governments
and between the British ambassador
at washington and the Irish minis
ter and for dealing with cases where
the respective functions might over
lap.


The British government was con-
fident the appointment would
strengthen the cordial relations with
the United States, without in any
way impairing the principle Of dip
lomatic unity of the whole British
empire.

Geuica, a young Italian, and his
eighteen.year-old bride Of two weeks,
were found riddIed with bullets in
bed in their home at 1913 Mott street
today. Police believe the double
murder was committed on Saturday.


Search is being made for the
girls father, who is missing.


Margaret Gandolfo Geuica was
one Of the bellies of the Italian
colony and her youthful husband
was boarder in her home. Her
mother was dead.


After the marriage a fortnight
ago Giuseppe Gandolfo, the girls
father, went to live with the bride
and groom. Family troubles de.
veloped and the father was ordered
out.


Neighbors told of hearing a VIC.
lent quarrel in the Geuica home
Saturday night, but no shots were
heard. Nor was Giuseppe seen to
leave the house.


The tragedy was discovered when
Thomas Gandolfo went to the Geuica
home to invite the bride and groom
to his own home for dinner. When
no one answered his knock he tried
the door and found it unlocked.


Finding the place apparently
empty Thomas started to investi-
gate. Lying amidst the tumbled
bed coverings were Carmilio and his
young wife, both bodies literally
riddled with bullets. Blood had
soaked through the thick mattress
and dripped upon the floor.

That is the riddle the average shop

cooker is retention of heat by inSu-
1ation-the surrounding Of the walls

heat; materials which in d refriger-
ator shut heat out and in fireless
cooker shut it in. 1t is not literally
true that the 'fireless cooker" cooks
without fire. for heat must be first
applied on the stove. and the cook
ing is finished without further heat
because the cooker retains that
which has already been applied. The
insulating materials used are uSu-
ally mineral wool, cork, asbestos and
excelsior. all poor heat conductors.

ding or covering for that material.

The victim of the plot, who went
with Zupke that night in the ex.
pectation of marrying him, wore

gown, white silk stockings, white
shoes and the dainty lingerie of a
bride, it was learned today. The

CHICAGO, November 20.-The Amer
lean Farm Bureau Federation esti-
mates that the value of American
farm products this year will exceed
ten billion dollars. over three billion
more than for the low year of 1922,
but four billion less than the high
mark reached in 1920. The estimates
are that the farmers in the wheat
belt, from Kansas to Montana, will
have about 25 per cent more income
and growers in the cotton belt about
per cent more.


This trend. according to the sur
vey, does not extend to the Pacific
Coast. where farmer income Is esti-
mated at 10 per cent less than that
of last year.


The tobacco belt, the corn belt and
the Western range States are believed
TO have secured at least as much
profit as they gained in 1923.

suit of the thrilling victory yesterday
of the South American soccer foot
ball team over Switzerland by
score of to 0.


The United States held the much
sought position in the stadium since
MAY is by virtue of the victory in
the rugby competition.

three goals better than the stalwart
team from Switzerland. The victory
was clean-cut and impressive, leav-
ing absolutely no doubt in the minds
of the record Olympic crowd that the
best team won.


Indomitable courage in the face of
tremendous odds was the only thing
that could be said for the Swiss. They
were outplayed. but they never said
die and continued fighting hopeless
ly lost battle until the referees
final whistle.

uous efforts on the part of the en-.

cursory examination showed that he
had probably suffered a broken back,
a broken leg and possibly a frac.
tured skull.

ton, said that he did not know

clared that eye witnesses said that

along safely just above the waters

dipped into the water and then
crashed against the bank.

a mass Of steel and wood and can.
vas. The wings were crumpled up
into a matchbox form. The huge
cabin was smithered into kindling
wood, and the rudders and tail
guard wwere gone entirely.


The crash happened about 1890
this afternoon.


Lieut.. Sprague said that for
NAL board of inquiry would be
summoned before the cause for the
accident was determined. Neither
Machinist CanqMar nor Morris
were seriously hurt.

progressing at good rate in the

Brookwood cemetery in England

terry at Romagne. Cuts have been

Will Plant Trees.

iantly in rescuing those thrown into

sank.

of the steamer a few seconds before
it disappeared beneath the waves.

asleep-a vast, pulsing body, quiet
under it's purple robe.

softly, her breath sweet with un-
uttered song. Far off and hushed

symphony.


Have a good time, Chickie?"

top of the hill. She felt his eyes

beautiful, fastened on her.

face, half knowing that it was

you?"

other. She saw his eyes. He an

Lowered his head ever so little

face-soft petals stained red and
sweet about her mouth.


They turned into the cloistered
aisle of Fair Oaks. They said
nothing. Her eyes were moist.
She wished to laugh but was
afraid that she might cry.


The life Jonothan wanted to
keep from her opened it's wild,
sweet voice in Chickie's heart.

NEW YORK. October S-Records
have fallen with regularity during
Ithe present worlds series ard yes
terday's game at the Polo Grounds
was no exception. Again the mark
for paid attendance was bettered
1929 p"ssing through the turnstiles

of, complimentary tickets.


In the first game Saturday all
records for attendance al Griffith
| Field in Washington were broken by
several thousand. On Sunday a few
hundred more squeezed into the park,
a again setting a record. Then the
Giants and Nationals came to play in
| the more spacious Polo Grounds and
Mondays game there found the
mark bettered for that park. Yester-
day that record also fell. There is
no way to determine just how many
would pay to see the present series
If there were accommodations. but
it is safe to say that the largest
stadium in the country would have to
turn away thousands.


Yesterdays crowd at the Polo
Grounds made hero out of a res
cued pitcher. The widest, loudest
and longest cheers of the day came
when George Mogridge strode from
the pitchers box to the Nationals
clubhouse door in the farthest cor
ner of the field. The lean hurlers
shoulders dropped. he hurried to get
away and he was disappointed, but he
might have walked with his eyes to
the sky, shoulders back and head
erect, for he was hero in the eyes
OF the bleacherites if not in his own.


For seven innings he had turned
back the giants with burning speed,
sharp breaking curves and a tanta-
lizing change of pace. Only three
hits had been made off him, one Of
them very scratchy. For six innings.
from the second through the seventh,
the Giants had been forced to face
the strongest pitching in the SERIES.
And then the great arm weakened.


The ball wouldn't go where it was
aimed and relief had to be called.
Mogridge's shoulders dropped but the
fans rose and cheered loud and long
as he walked off the field. Seldom
has rescued pitcher received such
an ovation and perhaps never when
playing away from home.


But the New York crowd yesterday
was backing Washington. Frisch's
brilliant fielding had won their plau-
dts and their admiration to the
Giants cause on Monday, but at heart
they were still ro-Washington. The
crowds cheers for the Giants had
been reluctant and given only when
forced. Yesterday the cheers for
Washington were spontaneous and
given gladly, joyously. When one
remembered the way that New York
fans urged the Giants on to victory
in the closing days of the National
League race, it seemed almost i'm
possible that the cheers could turn
against them in so short a time.


New York has seen many worlds
series and four of them have been in
the last four years, but the struggle
between the Giants and Nationals has
put new life into the throngs that
gather at the Polo Grounds and there
is none of the indifference that some-
times marked the crowds last season.
The thousands started streaming
into the stands at an early hour and
steady procession marched down
the aisles until every seat in the park
was filled and spectators overf1owed
into the passageways.

LONDON, May 5.-The gruesome
Eastbourne murder mystery, in
which an unidentified woman was
killed and her body dismembered.
was still unsolved today. Scotland
yard estimates that the murderer
spent at least two days cutting up
the body. Police officials said the
crime must have been committed
by fiend, probably a demented
person.


There is evidence that the killer
removed the heart and other vital
organs from the body and boiled
them. Even the marrow was re-
moved from the bones which were
sawed UP into grotesque shapes.


Flesh that remained was terribly
hacked. The head was missing,
making Identification more difficult.


Police spent many hours digging
up the garden of the EastbouFne
villa where the dismembered body
was found Saturday but made no
fresh discoveries. A man who had
rented the villa was detained by the
police but Scotland yard refuses
to say if there is any direct evil
dence against him.


A theory was advanced that the
slayer was a modern bluebeard''
who may have had a number of
female victims. Word was received
from Eastbourne this afternoon that
a baby's hand and arm had been
picked up on the beach a short dis
lance from Eastbourne.


Police are investigating to find If
there is any connection between
the killing of the baby and the
murder of the unidentified woman.

HAWKES. BAY. Newfoundland. Sep
tember 3.-The American Army air
planes on their world flight left here
for Pictou, Nova Scotia, at 12:40 pm,
Newfoundland daylight-saving time.
1t was raining and a southwest wind
was blowing 80 miles an hour when
the flyers hoped off. The clouds were
less than 1000 feet from the surface
and the machines kept at low alti-

waves.


The airmen were feeling none the
worse for their arduous experience
yesterday. when they had to fight
their way through fog, rain squalls
and a severe head wind on the latter
part Of their hop from Ice Tickle,
Labrador, 276 miles across the Lab
rador peninsula to this Newfoundland
town. They were feeling well and
were in fine spirits in anticipation of
their return later this week to the
soil of the United States.

Lieut.. Erik II. Nelson declared that
their long flight across the North
Atlantic from Reykjavik. Iceland, to
F'rede rikSda Greenland. had been
not only the longest but the most
difficult of the entire journey around
the world.


The flyers arrived at Hawkes. Bay
at 3:4s o'clock standard time yester-

flying weather. the American airmen
drove their planes steadily forward
under fine conditions until over Belle
Isle Straits and along the coast of
Newfoundland, where theT were
beset by rain and fog and a 30-mile

SPRINGFIELD, June 27--Success
attended the first organized attempt
to communicate by radio with the
international balloon racers while
in flight, and Westinghouse Sta
ton WBz at Springfield. Mass.
can lay claim to this signal honor.


The Springfield broadcasting sta
ton made special efforts to reach
Pilot Van Orlman Of the Balloon
Goodyear III. For several nights
following the ascension Of the com.
peting pilots, WBZ broadcast it's
programs with the hope Of enter
tanning the flyers and also courte.
ously transmitted official letters Of
cheer and messages Of encourage.
ment from friends of the American
pilot. Pilot Van Orman equipped
his balloon with receiving set,
and made every effort to get the
WBz call letters.


Until the American pilot made a
landing it was impossible to learn
whether or not he had received
anything from the Westinghouse
station. However, full substantial,
ton of his reception was given i'm
.mediately following his landing,
when WBZ received the following
cablegram:


Heard call letters, two thirty.
seven, Monday morning."


(Signed) Pilot Van Orman.


The reception was effected while
the Goodyear III was flying over
Holland. The cablegram was sent
from Amsterdam, Holland. There
Is difference Of six hours between
Holland and Eastern daylight saving
time. Pilot Van Arman evidently
heard a portion of the WBZ pro.
gram. which was broadcast between
$3.50 and O'clock p. m, on Sunday,
June Is.


This is the first time that any
effort has been made to reach com.
petitors in the International Balloon
Races by radio, and the success Of
WBZ's attempt to effect such com.
Inunications lists itself with another
Of the many accomplishments of
radio.

the lives of the firemen fighting the

ign nited by embers blown by a stiff

out serious damage. A warehouse,
under construction near the drydock,

ching.

cream into her pores and then

NEW YORK. October 11.-Score-

world series at the Griffith Stadium
in Washington. The crowd which
was attracted to City Hall Park,
where two large mechanical score
boards were recording the play by
play, was the largest since the world
series started, and more police were
called out to keep traffic open. The
subway entrances were blocked for a
time and passengers were forced to
emerge from the subway or enter it
by other kiosks than those in the
park.


Radio sets with loud speakers were
placed in many windows through the
city. Between Ninety-fourth and
Ninetyfifth street on Broadway a
loud speaker was placed in the win
dow on the second floor of small
store and the crowd it drew was so

stopping traffic. Few police were
stationed in this section. but before
the fifth inning was over a number of
bluecoatS were in evidence and re-





ditionS We're reported in many other
parts of the city.


Both the Nationals and the Giants
had large followings and the PARTISAN
ship apparently was equally divided.
This was especially noticeable in the
vicinity of City Hall, where, on the
whole, the crowds applauded every
good play by each team. When Man
ager Harris made his homer there
was big demonstration, but il did
not equal in volume the outburst

San Pedro, Calif.-Two prematur,
explosions killed three officers and
forty-five men of the battleship Mis-
sissippi and injured score of others,
and the menace of death still bounded
the crippled dreadnaught as she left
her dead and injured behind and head
ed out to sea to protect harbor life
and shipping from the peril of third
and imminently expected blast.


The first explosion occurred while
the Mississippi was engaged in target
practice off San Clemente island, for
ty-five miles from here, spreading
death among the eighty-five men in
Mo. 2 turret. Officers said the prema-
ture blast might have been due to
sailor giving the signal for the electric
flash igniting the charge in one of the
turret's fourteen-inch rifles before the
breech was properly closed, or may
have resulted from flare back"
caused when a fresh charge was being
loaded into the breech.


AS the stricken ship reached the
goal of its race for surgical assistance
the hospital ship Relief, just inside
the breakwater here-a second blast
rocked the vessel. The charge in the
damaged turret's second fourteen-inch
rifle exploded, hurting the steel pro-
jectie out to sea, and narrowly miss
ing the stern of the passenger liner
Yale, which was leaving the harbor
for San Diego.


Had the turret, which was revolving
ton or
Cured, remained in the same position
until the second blast, the projectile
would have crashed into the center of
the city of San Pedro. Fortunately the
turret had swung around so that its
guns pointed directly out to sea.


Nearly score more were injured
by the flare back that carried the ter
rifle charge backwards through the
breach of the gun instead of out
through the muzzle.


The gun crew were preparing to fire
as one unit in the great sea-fighter's
powerful broadside, when sailor
called for the electricity to be turned
on for the charge.


The switch was thrown to ignite the
shell before the breech was locked and
In another moment the interior of the
turret was Uttered with dead and dy-
ing.


A "flare-back" from one of the II
inch rifles in the turret ignited the
powder supply which practically wiped
out of existence the entire crew of the
turret room and also killed several men
in the upper handling room.


Four powder bags containing 45O
pounds of explosive each, were inside
the rifle turret, according to one of the
surviving sailors in the handling room
above, where several were also killed.


OF the injured, several sailors in the
passage spaces and handling room
above the turret were terribly burned
by gas and from the explosion.

Now that the various crews are

hears the usual amount of talk
about this style and that style of
sweep swinging.


One hears mention of the Court.
ney stroke, the Washington stroke,
the Jim Rice stroke and SO on. Yet
the fact is, none Of our great row.
ing coaches has ever adhered to a
fixed and rigid style Of rowing.


When 1t comes to distinct styles
Of rowing there are, broadly speak
ing, only two, the English and the
American.


You will see an English crew
bending forward when they catch
their oars in the water preparatory
to the pull, until their heads are
well down toward their knees hook
the water hard and pulling through
until their backs are almost down
in the bottom Of the boat.


You will see the American crew
dip their blades into the water,
their shoulders reaching not too
far forward, then pulling the oar
through with a snappy, powerful
leg drive, finishing the stroke with
the body only slightly beyond the
perpendicular.


Reasons for this difference in
stroke are mechanical The seat
upon which the British oarsman
sits slides only twenty inches as a
rule and the shoes in which the feet
rest are set some distance from the
seat. This makes the oarsman lean
far over in order to secure the
proper length to his stroke. Then,
at the finish, his slide stops sew
eral inches in front Of the thole
pins in which the oar rests and 80
he has to lie far back in order to
get a powerful finish.


This involves terrific punishment
upon the mid-section Of the body
and only oarsmen who have rowed
the stroke from boyhood can stand
the strain.


American crews have a much
longer slide-at Syracuse, for in.
stance, the slide has run to thirty
inches and the average is twenty.
six. The shoes are comparatively
close to the slide, 80 that whereas
the Englishman gets his power
from his waist and shoulders the
leg drive and from the shoulders.


In all American crews you will
see the pronounced leg drive, but
there never was a time when the
expert observer could watch a well
coached crew In action, not know
ing what university 1t represented,
and with certainty that that it is a
Wright eight, or a Spaeth eight,
or Leader eight, or another eight.

NEW YORK, September 13.-In q

Michael Wolf received a possible frac-
ture Of the skull and was taken to
Bellevue Hospital unconscious. Five
craps shooters were ar<Hsted.
Wolf, with his partners. James j.
Sullivan and James Walsh. were
! cruising about the neighborhood
looking for just what they found-a
craps game. -.


When they reached the engrossed
players, some one gave the warning
and the officers ordered all the young
men to. enter the garage. whore they
hoped to hold them until the arrival
of patrol wagon. For step or two
the craps shooters yielded. then sud-
denly" and without warning they
rushed the officers

their. revolvers, although they brought
their night sticks into play. When they
had been forced back to the gutter

past them into the street and picked
up cobblestones. The street Is un-
dergoing repairs at that spot. Soon

hurt, jim"


Needless Of the hurtling cobble-
stones Walsh and Sullivan rushed to
their comrades aid and were assist
ing him into the comparative safety

fell unconscious. They got him in
side, then grabbed five of the young
men, who later were charged with

once he saw. an automobile of

form the Federation of Soviet Rus
sian Republics" The argument of

long as England and other countries

favored only one vote for each coun-
try-represented.

ments on the incident as follows:
Democracy is an unknown word at
the International Postal Congress.
This has been shown by the tactless
and irrelevant criticisms of Soviet
Russia insinuated into the meetings
by the French delegation. There has
been some discussion as to how many
votes each country should have. In
1920 Switzerland proposed one each,
colony. When Russia asked one vote
was refused the extra votes, while
England was, given another vote for
Ireland. The question was a political
one and not a postal question, and
the chairman of the congress, Gen.
Williamson of England, supports this
anti bolshevist policy"

CHICAGO, April 14-Sanction of
steel shaft golf clubs by the United
States Golf Association removed the
only open difference between that
body rand the Western Golf Associa-
tion, which, after thorough trials two
years ago, authorized the use of steel
shaft clubs in tournaments.


Shortly after metal shafts were
placed on the market objection was
raised to their use on the ground that
they furnished u mechanical aid to
long and straight driving The
makers declared that while the shafts
were not inferior to first-class rick
ory they did not of themselves make
a good driver out of mediocre golfer,
but that the steel shaft retained it's
elasticity and torsional spring indef-
nitely, while hickory gradually de-
terioriated and had to be replaced.


In the Western Golf Association
trials of the metal shaft such star
players as Bob Macdonald, Jock
Hutchison and Chick Evans drove
many balls with both steel and wood
shafts. The results showed that while
apparently the steel shaft club kept
the heeled or toed shot a trifle
straighter, the distance was cut CON
siderably. These experts got better
distance with hickory shafts and ex-
pressed a preference for them, but
asserted that for general use the uni
formity of metal shafts made them
desirable. as the ordinary player could
not always select fine wooden handles.

NEW YORK, March Perhaps
the financial millennium is just
around the corner.


A scheme has been devised to con.
troll the babbling tongues Of stock
statesmen.


Through the years, promoters
have Visualized the most favorable
possible outcome Of their dreams,
and have commissioned statesmen
to sell these exaggerated hopes and
aspirations to. gullible public in
the form of neatly engraved stock
certificates. 2.>,


Working ON the dubious theory
that they had to eat and live, stock
statesmen went the easiest way,
and to facilitate sales amplified and
embroidered a hundred fold in many
instances the conceptions of their
chiefs. What the promoter sug-
gested, they promised. Where the
promoter said may" the salsemen
would assert will"


Through excessive exaggeration
and through the processes of tine
which revealed default on promises
wickedly made, the profession Of
vending promotion stocks became
discredited. The press. better bust
ness bureaus, the United States
Treasury and the banks used their
influence to check such campaigns
which separated the unknowing
from their savings.


This counter movement Of educa-
ton has temporarily developed
greater resistance to the efforts of
the conventional stock statesmen.


Thus the virtuous and the wicked
have been suffering alike from the
skepticism of the general public.


But for progress, experiment and
innovation need to be financed, The
great mechanical revolutions which
changed our mode of living and
which seem commonplace enough
now were far from sure things
when inventors first created them
out of their imagination. However,
industrial pioneering, based on trial
and error, though exceedingly de-
sirable and necessary for the COM
munity, entail hazards far too great
to justify the employment of the
meager funds of widows and others
who cannot, in any circumstances,
afford to lose.


The investor needs to look to
tested achievements for safety Of
principal and regularity of income,
which should be his goal. New
ideas and inventions, whose COM
mercial success remains to be DEM
onstrated, are not in this category.


Even the meritorious promoter
has an uphill fight, and his finan-
cial supporters share the burden.
Thousands succumb before one sue
ceeds magnificently, but the mem
DRY of the one conspicuous success
impels countless others to under
take the struggle.

been making every effort to effect the
capture of the outlaws.

Santiago had fortified himself to with
stand the advance of the constabu-
larry. When the troops advanced the
outlaws started the battle by opening
with heavy rife fire from three sides

piled with deadly effect. Santiago,
seeing that the tide was turning
against the defenders, escaped to the
mountains with five rifles.


The remaining Moro outlaws con-
tinued the fight.

native spies felt confident of finding
Santiago.

WHY do cowboys wear the large


handkerchiefs around their
necks? Because it is custom, or
just for looks?


Neither" says Allene Ray, the new
serial star, and she thus started an
argument with her company.


Finally Miss Ray asked an old cow
boy, who had been a cattle puncher
many years. He explained that the
wearing of the handkerchiefs was a
custom now, but in the good old
days" while herding cattle or driving
them any great distance they usually
had to pass through sections of alkaii
country. The dust stirred up by the
trotting cattle nearly suffocated the
cowboys. The handkerchiefs were
then brought into use by placing
them in bandit fashion just below the
eyes, so that the wearer could
breathe freely without sucking the
dust into his lungs. After the
alkali area had been passed, the
handkerchief would be pulled down
and left around the neck.

ANTIETAM BATTLEFIELD, Sep
tember 10.-The marines here are
planning to give their share of well
come to the world flyers when they
pass here on their way to Moundsville,
Ohio.

arranged. Everything that can fly
will take off as they approach and
escort them for several miles. All
the big guns will be fired, and bombs
will be dropped all around.

thawing out after the cold night.
Frost was reported in several OF the
encampments, but the marines are
used to all sorts of weather, and
now that the sun is shining bright
ly are feeling pretty clipper and in
readiness for the big show Friday.
Bayonet drills are the program today,
and they are hard at work.


Tomorrow is the last dress fehear-
sal, and the following day the
marines expect to do Lees and
McClellan's armies one better.

guns, stood back of Hanson, who

ing the rescue.

the group of six stowaways, who
were in chains, and shuff1ed off the
ship. The stowaways were taken
to Ellis Island.

NEW YORK, August 2S.-Six more
storm-hammered ships, additional
victims of the Sunday-to-Tuesday
hurricane which cut a great swath
from the south to the north Atlantic,
made port early today, bearing fur
ther witness of the storms fury.


The ships coming in today were
smaller than the battered passenger
liners which arrived yesterday, first
OF the storms victims to make port.
Those yesterday were the White Star
liners Arabic and Homeric, the Mum
son liner Munargo, the Orizaba of the
Ward line, and the Italian steamship
Giuseppe Verdi and the Munson ship
Aundelta.


Captain Is Lost.


Tho Nordfarer, 2,500-ton Danish
cargo boat, arrived first today. When
5ust south of Cape Hatteras Monday
night the stanch little ship was al
most crushed under the weight of the
waters that rolled over her. The mad
hurricane, in which a 120-mile-an-
hour wind kicked up waves 40 and
so feet in height, caught the Nord-
farer in its greatest fury. gar
gantuan wave struck her bow on and
washed away the bridge, carrying
Capt. M. J. Madsen with it.


Behind the Nordfarer. the San
Pablo, from Tela. Hor duras, made
her entry. She suffered the loss of
her lifeboats and all the loose articles
that had been on deck.


Next came the British steamer In
dian Prince. from Santos, Brazil. She
was overtaken by the storm 500 miles
south of Hatteras. Her crew told a
tale of one of their number being
swept from the decks by a titanic
wave, which washed him aboard
again when a fragment Of the hur-
ricane wind veered and hurled the
water back. The steamers decks and
upper works were badly damaged.


Has Slight Damage.


In quick succession there follow ed
the San Jose, from West Indian ports
the Corsican Prince. out of Buenos
Aires, and the Commodore Rollins
from Kingston, Jamaica. The San
Jose was only slightly damaged. The
Corsican Prince suffered a bit more
damage. although she also got mixed
with the tail of the storm. The Rol-
Inns got but minor injuries. as she
just skirted the storms edge.


In strange contrast. the Fort Vic
toria came into port as the seventh
arrival. making jaunty entry, her
off1cers reporting an excellent trip
from Bermuda. The Fort Victoria
just nOSSO the eQSe OF the hurricane
belt.


Capt. Hickson of the Arabic, whose
vessel and passengers were the major
victims, said the wind at times at
tanned an, intensity OF 120 miles an
hour, and Capt. Metcalf Of the Ho-
meric, sister White Star liner of the
Arabic, asserted it was the worst
within his memory.


Both said that while firemen pushed
the engines to capacity to keep the
vessels bows heading into the wind,
they were stopped dead in their
tracks, with cross-waves pounding at
their sides. The Arabic on numerous
occasions. leaned dangerously close to
the 45 degree angle.


The Giuseppe Verdi, whose captain
had brought her from Genoa to meet
the storm, exhibited dent in smoke
stack so feet above the water line.


Had $50 Casualties.


The Arabic had an estimated cas-.
ualty list of more than $50, with SO
persons who required treatment. OF
these, 33 were under the care of sur
geons. when the vessel docked, met
by ambulances previously summoned
by wireless.


High tribute was paid by the pas
sengers to the gallantry and fearless
ness Of the crew in restoring order,
aiding passengers at their own peril

ments melted by rumors from
Manila attacked a large rice mill at

damaging the property before the
constabulary could control them.


force of $50 constabulary has ar

Gov. Gen. Wood and his assurance
that they would not be molested


For II hours now within the city

but the Chinese uneasiness Is shared
by others because of the manner in
which the police handled the rioters.
Official delays and temporizing have
twisted the whole situation into a
national issue with political aspects.

crowds in the Mehan Gardens.

ing out gangs who were arrested dur
ing the riot. If trials ever occur con-
victions will be doubtful, because II
is practically impossible to obtain
evidence. Therefore the scapa BILE
conclusion shared by the best opinions
of the most reputable persons is that
the rabble will feel safe in the future
In making similar attacks, and that
without strict constabulary control
occasional depredations upon isolated
chinese towns will be frequent
i'rompt police action without political
intervention would not involve a

Three Italian mountain climbers

rience yesterday of hanging five

ped, dragging the others with him

rock as they went over the, edge

on the rope attempted to get a
footing until his comrades shouted
that he risked loosening their
support.

below and a rescue party was dis
patched. The trio were pulled up
with great difficulty and after
long efforts, and were brought to
Chamonix. One had a broken leg
and the others were covered with
bruises.

There will be rejoicing over the
rescue Of Lieut.. Locatelli, the Italian
aviator, who, setting out from Ice
land with the American globe flyers,
lost contact with them and disap-
peared before they reached Green
land. There was reason to believe
that Locatelli had been forced to
descend, and it was feared that he
would not be found, as the sea is
rough and cold, with much ice afloat.
There were four men on the Italian
plane, which carried a heavy store Of
fuel and other supplies. Evidently
the long hop from Iceland was too
much for it, while the two American
planes were making their way safely
to their chosen landing point.


This rescue is additional assurance
that long distance flying is not neces-
sarily deadly risk. Since this series
Of globe flights started several avi-
ators have been forced down in
isolated places, and all of them have
been rescued. Martin crashed into a
mountain in the Aleutian peninsula,
and after several days made his way
back to a station where he was given
succor. MacLaren, the British flyer,
was forced to descend off the Japa-
nese coast, and was later located and
aided back to mainland. One Of the
three remaining American planes
was forced down between the Ork-
neys and Iceland, but the flyers were
promptly picked up, though their
plane was wrecked. In this last case
the rescuers were close at hand.
Locatell and his comrades might
have persisted off the Greenland coast
but for the presence Of the American
convoy fleet, which Immediately put
of and secured the waters for him.

halte Many automobiles are stranded

chester, to the north, and Waynes-
boro, to the south: Tourists aband oned

GREENVILLE, Ala, April 3d.
Four persons, all members of one
family, were injured in a tornado
which struck Greenville and vicinity
early this morning. Property damage
is estimated at $4,000. Two negroes
are reported missing and are thought
to have been killed.


The injured are: Mrs. E. c. Poole
and three children. who were buried
beneath the debris of their home
when it was blown down while they
were asleep. Miss Lucille Poole was
the most serious injured, although
all are expected to recover


The tornado cut a path a half mile
wide through the town. Buildings
destroyed include the Louisville and
Nashville freight depot, two cotton
warehouses of the Planters Mer-
camille Company, a blacksmith shop
and several negro dwellings. The
First Baptist Church was badly
damaged. At least sixty buildings
were badly damaged. Nearly all
wires from Greenville were out and
the power lines were down.


A negro man named Smith is be-
lieved to have persisted in the flames
that burned his little shack following
its destruction by the wind. A negro
girl also is reported missing

DANZIG. July 5.-English dancing
girls. who disappeared like magic
from the stages of continental
Europe in August. 1914. have begun
to return to their former fields of
activity, and have even invaded
Russia where they were always
popular prior to the war. 1t has
been nearly ten years since the
London dancers have been seen to
any extent in the cities of central
Europe, although at intervals during
the war there were a few troupes
appearing in Paris, Madrid Rome
and some other places.


Throughout Europe before the
war. wherever there were variety
theaters or music halls. there were
English dancing girls. known for
their sprightly dancing often COM
bined with singing stunts. Even in
old st. Petersburg and Moscow, the
home of the Russian ballet, the dane
ing girls from London were always
well received.


This spring, a troupe toured the
Scandinavian cities and the Baltic
states and from Danzig went on to
Leningrad, where there had been
no English performers since the
soviets came into power. Later the
dancers will visit Warsaw, Bucharest
Budapest, Vienna and numerous
other cities. Several other troupes
from London also took the road this
spring, and have been appearing in
Rotterdam, Stockholm, Copenhagen,
Berlin and other northern cities.

NEW YORK, Oct. 21.-The theory
that fifteen-year-old Julia Hannigan,
pretty Brooklyn high school girl,
has been strangled and her body
hidden away, was considered by
police today, following the discovery
in. the cellar of the missing girls
home of all her clothes except her
silk stockings.


Detectives, recalling the cellar
murder of Ruth Cruger, searched
the Hannigan cellar and unearthed
the clothing under boards.


Celia Hannigan, an older sister.
following Julia's disappearance, told
police she heard a noise in the
cellar the night before and saw a
man running away.


Police believe the man may have
placed the clothing in the cellar
at that time, or may have returned
later to do so.


Police called to investigate Julia's
disappearance, found she had not
been in school for two weeks. Mrs.
Hannigan was unaware of this.
